questions.question: Why are pairwise preference labels often preferred over absolute scalar ratings when training reward models for language models?
questions.choice_A: Pairwise comparisons reduce inter-annotator calibration issues by asking only which of two options is better.
questions.choice_B: Absolute scalar ratings are harder to use with gradient-based methods than pairwise labels.
questions.choice_C: Pairwise labels guarantee transitive preferences across the dataset.
questions.choice_D: Pairwise data is always cheaper to collect than scalar ratings.

questions.question: In a Bradley–Terry-style preference model for reward learning, what is the key probabilistic assumption connecting latent rewards to observed pairwise preferences?
questions.choice_A: The probability that response i is preferred to j is a logistic function of the difference in their latent rewards.
questions.choice_B: Annotators deterministically choose the response with the higher reward score.
questions.choice_C: Latent rewards are uniformly distributed across all responses.
questions.choice_D: Preferences are independent of the prompt/context and depend only on response length.

questions.question: What is the central idea behind Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) compared to standard RLHF with a reward model and PPO?
questions.choice_A: DPO replaces the policy with a value function to simplify credit assignment.
questions.choice_B: DPO optimizes a scalar KL divergence without using preferences.
questions.choice_C: DPO directly adjusts the policy to match observed pairwise preferences via a log-ratio objective, avoiding an explicit RL loop.
questions.choice_D: DPO requires on-policy rollouts for every gradient step.

questions.question: Which annotator interface design choice most effectively reduces position/order bias in pairwise preference collection?
questions.choice_A: Always display the model’s top-ranked response first.
questions.choice_B: Show responses in order of increasing length.
questions.choice_C: Highlight stylistic features in the preferred option.
questions.choice_D: Randomize the left/right or top/bottom positions of candidate responses for each comparison.

questions.question: Which quality-control strategy best detects systematic annotator mistakes in preference data at scale?
questions.choice_A: Increasing model sampling temperature during data collection.
questions.choice_B: Embedding gold-standard checks and monitoring inter-annotator agreement to trigger adjudication.
questions.choice_C: Aggregating preferences using simple majority vote only.
questions.choice_D: Allowing annotators to skip any hard example with no review.

questions.question: What best characterizes Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT) for aligning language models?
questions.choice_A: Sample multiple candidate outputs, filter them by a reward model or rule set, and fine-tune only on the accepted samples.
questions.choice_B: Jointly train the policy and reward model end-to-end with backpropagation through the reward.
questions.choice_C: Use a value function to assign step-wise credit and update the policy with TD learning.
questions.choice_D: Collect human preferences online during PPO updates.

questions.question: What does “calibration” of a reward or preference model primarily mean in this context?
questions.choice_A: The model’s scores are as large as possible on the training data.
questions.choice_B: The model produces the same score distributions across all prompts.
questions.choice_C: The model’s predicted preference probabilities reflect the empirical frequencies with which humans would prefer those options.
questions.choice_D: The model’s scores exactly match human-provided scalar ratings.

questions.question: Which scenario illustrates a generalization failure of a learned reward model?
questions.choice_A: The model assigns identical scores to duplicate responses.
questions.choice_B: The model assigns high reward to outputs exploiting spurious stylistic cues that correlate with quality in training data but not out-of-domain.
questions.choice_C: The model’s variance estimates increase on harder examples.
questions.choice_D: The model maintains consistency under paraphrasing.

questions.question: How does process supervision differ from outcome supervision when designing reward signals for alignment?
questions.choice_A: Process supervision evaluates intermediate reasoning steps or methodology, not just final outputs.
questions.choice_B: Outcome supervision only scores the first token of the output.
questions.choice_C: Process supervision ignores the reasoning chain and focuses on final correctness.
questions.choice_D: Outcome supervision provides dense, step-wise rewards during generation.

questions.question: What is a principled approach to handling noisy or inconsistent pairwise labels from multiple annotators?
questions.choice_A: Model annotator reliabilities or label noise explicitly (e.g., via Bayesian or EM approaches) and incorporate uncertainty into training.
questions.choice_B: Discard any example where annotators disagree to ensure purity of the dataset.
questions.choice_C: Upsample examples with high disagreement to dominate training.
questions.choice_D: Assume all annotators are equally reliable and treat ties as random coin flips.

questions.question: Which pairwise loss aligns most directly with a probabilistic interpretation of preferences under a Bradley–Terry model?
questions.choice_A: Logistic (cross-entropy) loss on the difference of latent rewards.
questions.choice_B: Squared error between raw logits and labels.
questions.choice_C: Hinge loss with a fixed safety margin.
questions.choice_D: 0-1 loss on predicted preference identity.

questions.question: How can uncertainty estimates from a reward model be used to improve policy training?
questions.choice_A: They are not useful; only point estimates of reward matter.
questions.choice_B: Use them to always pick the most uncertain examples for training, ignoring confident ones.
questions.choice_C: Drive risk-sensitive or conservative updates (e.g., down-weight high-uncertainty regions or explore to reduce uncertainty).
questions.choice_D: Replace the reward model with an uncertainty-only objective.

questions.question: What is a common risk when applying a reward model trained on one domain (e.g., summarization) to another (e.g., code generation)?
questions.choice_A: The reward model will automatically adapt to the new domain without performance loss.
questions.choice_B: The reward’s scale will become exactly zero-centered in the new domain.
questions.choice_C: The pairwise training objective becomes non-convex.
questions.choice_D: Distribution shift can cause misalignment; mitigation includes domain-diverse training, calibration checks, and OOD detection.

questions.question: When collecting K-way preferences (K > 2) for a prompt, what is a trade-off of converting them to all pairwise comparisons?
questions.choice_A: It reduces statistical efficiency because fewer labels are used per prompt.
questions.choice_B: It increases signal by using more comparisons but introduces dependency among pairs and potential sampling bias if pairs are not balanced.
questions.choice_C: It guarantees transitivity in the aggregated preferences.
questions.choice_D: It eliminates the need for a link function like the logistic.

questions.question: How can a preference model handle intransitive human judgments (A > B, B > C, but C > A) observed in the data?
questions.choice_A: By modeling latent utilities with noise (e.g., Thurstone/BT frameworks), which can accommodate cyclic comparisons probabilistically.
questions.choice_B: By discarding all examples until transitivity holds globally.
questions.choice_C: By converting to scalar ratings post hoc and taking the mean.
questions.choice_D: By assuming annotator errors are impossible.

questions.question: Which compensation and workflow practice most reliably promotes high-quality preference annotations?
questions.choice_A: Pay per item with incentives for speed only.
questions.choice_B: Hide instructions to reduce priming effects.
questions.choice_C: Hourly pay with calibrated workload, clear rubrics, qualification tests, and bonuses tied to verified quality checks.
questions.choice_D: Use a single annotator to ensure consistency.

questions.question: Compared to DPO, which is a typical computational cost characteristic of Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT) during data generation?
questions.choice_A: RFT requires backpropagating through the reward model at inference time.
questions.choice_B: RFT often requires generating many candidates per prompt to filter, increasing sampling cost.
questions.choice_C: RFT eliminates the need to sample any candidates during training.
questions.choice_D: RFT must use on-policy rollouts for each gradient step.

questions.question: Which evaluation best probes the robustness of a reward model to superficial changes in text that preserve meaning?
questions.choice_A: Measuring accuracy on the training set only.
questions.choice_B: Counting the number of tokens in each response.
questions.choice_C: Testing on out-of-domain tasks without controlling for semantics.
questions.choice_D: Paraphrase consistency tests: apply meaning-preserving transformations and check preference order stability.

questions.question: When constructing preference datasets for multi-turn conversations, what is critical to avoid context-related artifacts?
questions.choice_A: Include the full conversation history, system instructions, and user intent so annotators judge responses within the correct context.
questions.choice_B: Only present the last user message to simplify annotation.
questions.choice_C: Truncate responses to a fixed length regardless of content.
questions.choice_D: Shuffle turns to reduce position bias across the whole dialog.

questions.question: What is a potential pitfall of using step-wise process rewards on chain-of-thought reasoning traces?
questions.choice_A: They cannot be combined with outcome rewards.
questions.choice_B: They guarantee truthful intermediate steps even when outcomes are wrong.
questions.choice_C: They can mis-specify credit, incentivizing verbose or instrumentally deceptive intermediate steps that game the reward.
questions.choice_D: They eliminate the need for any outcome evaluation.
